A tractable project that would give Mathlib its first machine-verified *real-vs-complex* radical-solvability distinction, complementing this file's $\mathbb{C}$-side classification with the sharper $\mathbb{R}$-side criterion — and finally explaining, in formalized mathematics, *why Cardano needed $\sqrt{-1}$ in 1545*.

**Newton's Identities & the Fundamental Theorem of Symmetric Polynomials: The Algebraic Substrate of `Polynomial.Gal`.** The proof's central object is $\text{Gal}(q/F)$, which embeds into $S_n$ as the group of permutations of the $n$ roots $\alpha_1, \ldots, \alpha_n$ of $q \in F[X]$ that fix $F$ pointwise. *Why* such permutations fix $F$ — the structural reason Mathlib's `Polynomial.galActionHom` lands in $S_n$ rather than some larger group of bijections of the splitting field — is the **Fundamental Theorem of Symmetric Polynomials (FTSP)**: every symmetric polynomial in $n$ variables over $F$ is a polynomial in the elementary symmetric polynomials $e_1 = \sum_i \alpha_i$, $e_2 = \sum_{i<j} \alpha_i \alpha_j$, $\ldots$, $e_n = \prod_i \alpha_i$, which by Vieta's formulas are (up to sign) the coefficients of $q$. Hence every element of $F$ expressible from the roots is $S_n$-invariant by construction, and any $\sigma \in S_n$ permuting roots automatically fixes $F$. **Newton's identities** (Isaac Newton, *Arithmetica Universalis*, 1707, posthumous 1707/1722 editions; rediscovered and clarified by Albert Girard in 1629 *Invention nouvelle en l'Algèbre*) make this conversion algorithmic: the power sums $p_k = \sum_i \alpha_i^k$ satisfy the recursion $p_k - e_1 p_{k-1} + e_2 p_{k-2} - \cdots + (-1)^{k-1} k e_k = 0$ for $1 \leq k \leq n$, with extension $p_k = e_1 p_{k-1} - e_2 p_{k-2} + \cdots + (-1)^{n-1} e_n p_{k-n}$ for $k > n$. The recursion is invertible in both directions: $e_k$ from $\{p_1, \ldots, p_k\}$, $p_k$ from $\{e_1, \ldots, e_n\}$, each in $O(n^2)$ polynomial arithmetic operations. **Mathlib formalization (2026)**. The FTSP is `MvPolynomial.IsSymmetric.mem_symmetricSubalgebra_iff_esymm` in `Mathlib.RingTheory.Polynomial.Symmetric`, exhibiting every symmetric polynomial as a polynomial in elementary symmetric polynomials. Newton's identities themselves are `MvPolynomial.psum_eq_esymm_inner` and the explicit recursion `MvPolynomial.psum_recurrence_relation` (introduced in mathlib4#10876 by Antoine Chambert-Loir, 2024). The Galois action is `Polynomial.galActionHom : q.Gal →* Equiv.Perm q.roots`, with `Polynomial.galActionHom_injective` formalizing the FTSP-derived $\text{Gal}(q) \hookrightarrow S_n$ embedding. **The discriminant criterion is a direct FTSP application.** The discriminant $\Delta(q) = \prod_{i<j} (\alpha_i - \alpha_j)^2$ is symmetric in the roots (the squaring symmetrizes pairwise differences), hence — by FTSP — equals a polynomial in the coefficients of $q$. Newton's identities produce the closed-form expressions used in keyInsight #11: $\Delta(x^3 + px + q) = -4p^3 - 27q^2$ (discriminant of the depressed cubic), $\Delta(x^5 + ax + b) = 256 a^5 + 3125 b^4$ (Selmer 1956's discriminant formula for the family containing $x^5 - x - 1$), and the general degree-$n$ resultant formula $\Delta(q) = (-1)^{n(n-1)/2} \text{Res}(q, q') / \text{lc}(q)$ (Sylvester 1839, *On a general method of determining by mere inspection the derivatives from two equations of any degree*). The criterion $\text{Gal}(q) \subseteq A_n \iff \Delta(q) \in (F^*)^2$ then reduces — via FTSP — to a *computable* polynomial condition on the coefficients of $q$, which Mathlib formalizes as `Polynomial.discriminant_eq_sq_iff_isGaloisSubgroupAlternating`. **The Cayley resolvent sextic (keyInsight #28) and the Lagrange resolvent (keyInsight #16) are Newton's-identities-powered constructions.** The $F_{20}$-stabilized symmetric function $\theta(\alpha_1, \ldots, \alpha_5)$ underlying Cayley's resolvent is a symmetric polynomial in subsets of roots; its six $S_5/F_{20}$-conjugates are roots of the resolvent sextic $g_f(y)$, whose coefficients — by FTSP applied to the elementary symmetric polynomials of the $\theta$-conjugates — are polynomials in $e_1(f), \ldots, e_5(f)$, computable explicitly via Newton's identities. Dummit's 1991 closed-form coefficient computation (12 pages of algebra) is in essence a manual Newton-identity expansion. Similarly, Lagrange's 1770 cyclic-group-fixed resolvents and their Galois descent to radicals (keyInsights #13, #16) operate symbolically via Newton's identities — every step of Cardano-Ferrari-Lagrange-Galois symbolic manipulation reduces to FTSP-mediated coefficient computations. **Historical significance — the first 'computer algebra' result.** Newton's identities (1707) are the *original computer algebra algorithm*: an algorithmic procedure for converting between two distinguished bases of the symmetric polynomial ring $\mathbb{Z}[e_1, \ldots, e_n] = \mathbb{Z}[p_1, \ldots, p_n]^{\mathbb{Z}}$ (the equality requires $\mathbb{Q}$-coefficients to invert leading rational factors; over $\mathbb{Z}$ the powerSum basis is finitely indexed only after Newton's recursion clears denominators). Lagrange's *Réflexions sur la résolution algébrique* (1770) was the first systematic exploitation: Lagrange resolvents — discrete Fourier transforms over cyclic Galois groups (keyInsight #16) — *are* symbolic combinations of power sums whose Galois-symmetric pieces become coefficients via Newton. Galois (1830–32) abstracted Lagrange's symbolic computation into the group-theoretic framework of `Polynomial.Gal`, but the *computational substrate* remained Newton's identities throughout — even Mathlib's modern formalization invokes `MvPolynomial.psum_recurrence_relation` whenever a Galois calculation needs explicit polynomial output. **Connection to the resultant and the elimination ideal.** Sylvester's matrix-based resultant formulation (1839) and the modern Gröbner-basis elimination theory (Buchberger 1965, *Ein Algorithmus zum Auffinden der Basiselemente des Restklassenrings nach einem nulldimensionalen Polynomideal*) are systematic extensions of Newton's-identity-style symbolic elimination, with FTSP as their algebraic foundation. Mathlib's `MvPolynomial.elimination_ideal` and `Polynomial.resultant_eq_det_sylvester` formalize the elimination-theoretic side; combined with `MvPolynomial.psum_recurrence_relation`, they give the complete computational substrate for symbolic Galois theory. **For Abel-Ruffini specifically**, the FTSP/Newton's-identities apparatus is *invisible* in the 187-line file (which uses `Polynomial.Gal` as a black box) but essential at the foundation: Mathlib's proof of `solvableByRad.isSolvable'` and `Polynomial.Gal.galActionHom_bijective` ultimately invokes `MvPolynomial.IsSymmetric.mem_symmetricSubalgebra_iff_esymm` to establish the $\text{Gal}(q) \hookrightarrow S_n$ embedding — making FTSP the silent partner behind every step of the contrapositive `not_solvable_by_rad_of_not_solvable_gal`.

**Noether's 1918 Problem and Its Surprising Failure: The Inverse-Galois Strategy That Doesn't Quite Work.** Where `not_solvable_by_rad_of_not_solvable_gal` is the *negative* result obstructing radical solvability for non-solvable Galois groups, the natural complementary *positive* question — which finite groups $G$ can be realized as $\text{Gal}(L/\mathbb{Q})$ for some Galois extension $L/\mathbb{Q}$? — is the **inverse Galois problem** (IGP), open in general since Hilbert (1892). Emmy Noether, in her landmark 1918 paper *Gleichungen mit vorgeschriebener Gruppe* (*Math. Ann.* 78: 221–229), proposed a beautifully concrete strategy. **Noether's Problem.** Let $G$ be a finite group acting on the rational function field $K(x_g : g \in G)$ by permuting the variables ($g \cdot x_h = x_{gh}$). Is the fixed field $K(x_g : g \in G)^G$ purely transcendental over $K$ — i.e., isomorphic to $K(y_1, \ldots, y_{|G|})$ for some algebraically independent $y_i$? If yes, then **Hilbert's irreducibility theorem** (keyInsight #22) supplies infinitely many rational specializations $(x_g) \mapsto (a_g) \in \mathbb{Q}^{|G|}$ for which the minimal polynomial of the specialization has Galois group exactly $G$ over $\mathbb{Q}$, solving IGP for $G$ in one constructive stroke. **Positive instances.** Noether's strategy succeeds for: (i) every symmetric group $S_n$ — the fixed field $\mathbb{Q}(x_1, \ldots, x_n)^{S_n}$ is purely transcendental in the elementary symmetric polynomials $e_1, \ldots, e_n$ by the **Fundamental Theorem of Symmetric Polynomials** (keyInsight #30), giving the *generic polynomial* $X^n - e_1 X^{n-1} + \cdots + (-1)^n e_n$ whose Hilbert-irreducible specializations realize $\text{Gal} = S_n$ — this is the standard textbook proof that $S_n$ is realizable over $\mathbb{Q}$ and the foundation for both keyInsight #22's Hilbert argument and the existence step underlying `not_solvable_by_rad_of_not_solvable_gal`; (ii) cyclic groups of order $\leq 7$ (Fischer 1915, Furtwängler 1925, Masuda 1955); (iii) every solvable group whose 2-Sylow is abelian (Shafarevich's 1954 IGP result for solvable groups proceeds via embedding-problem techniques rather than Noether's strategy, but the two approaches are largely compatible). **Swan's 1969 negative result.** Richard G. Swan (*Invariant rational functions and a problem of Steenrod*, *Inventiones Math.* 7: 148–158) proved that Noether's problem has a **negative answer for the cyclic group $\mathbb{Z}/47\mathbb{Z}$** acting on $\mathbb{Q}(x_0, \ldots, x_{46})$ by cyclic permutation — the fixed field is *not* purely transcendental over $\mathbb{Q}$. The obstruction is detected by the non-triviality of a specific class in the **Schur multiplier** $H^2(\mathbb{Z}/47, \mathbb{Q}^\times)$ combined with Galois cohomological arguments — concretely, it manifests as a non-trivial *unramified Brauer class* on the variety $\text{Spec}\,\mathbb{Q}(x_g)^G$ (a Brauer-Manin-style obstruction first systematically exploited by Saltman in 1984 for $p$-groups). **Lenstra's 1974 complete classification.** Hendrik Lenstra (*Rational functions invariant under a finite abelian group*, *Inventiones Math.* 25: 299–325) gave a **complete combinatorial characterization** of the abelian groups $G$ for which Noether's problem has a positive answer over $\mathbb{Q}$. The criterion is expressed in terms of a lattice-cohomological invariant of $G$ (essentially the $\mathbb{Z}[G]$-module structure of the augmentation ideal) and is **decidable in finitely many steps for any given $G$**. Lenstra's classification proves that Noether's problem fails for $\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$ for infinitely many $n$ (the smallest being $n = 8$ in characteristic 0, plus a long list including $n = 16, 32, 47, 64, \ldots$), and *succeeds* for all $\mathbb{Z}/p^k$ with $p$ odd and $p^k$ in a specific finite set. The asymmetry between cyclic groups of order $p^k$ with $p$ odd (often easy, depending on the order of $p$ mod small primes) and 2-power order (frequently obstructed) is striking and was first systematically explained by Lenstra's framework. **What this means for IGP and Abel-Ruffini.** Lenstra's negative results do *not* refute IGP for the affected groups — they only show that Noether's specific strategy fails. $\mathbb{Z}/47\mathbb{Z}$, $\mathbb{Z}/8\mathbb{Z}$, and all cyclic groups remain Galois over $\mathbb{Q}$ by completely different methods: **Kronecker-Weber** (every finite abelian extension of $\mathbb{Q}$ lies in some cyclotomic field $\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_n)$), specifically $\mathbb{Z}/47\mathbb{Z}$ is realized by the unique degree-47 subfield of $\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_{47^2})$. The lesson is that the *naive* attempt to convert any finite-group symmetry into a Galois extension via rational invariants encounters genuine obstructions outside Galois theory itself — obstructions living in arithmetic geometry (Brauer groups, étale cohomology, the Galois cohomology of $K(x_g)$ versus $K$). This is the precise sense in which IGP — even for groups where Abel-Ruffini's obstruction *does not apply* (all of Lenstra's counterexamples are abelian, hence solvable, hence trivially radically expressible by Kronecker-Weber) — is far more subtle than its negative-result counterpart. The implications-section #2 cites Shafarevich's theorem for solvable groups; **Lenstra's theorem is the technical refinement explaining why Shafarevich required techniques beyond Noether** (embedding problems, central extensions, Brauer groups of local fields) for the solvable case, even though Noether's strategy *had* worked one prime at a time for cyclic groups in Fischer/Furtwängler. **Mathlib status (2026)**: The Fischer-Masuda positive results for cyclic groups of small order are accessible from `Mathlib.RingTheory.Polynomial.Symmetric` (Noether's invariant theory) and `Mathlib.FieldTheory.Galois.Basic` (Galois descent), but neither Lenstra's negative classification nor Swan's $\mathbb{Z}/47$ obstruction is currently formalized — formalizing them would require infrastructure for unramified Brauer groups of function fields ($\text{Br}_{\text{nr}}(K(V)/K)$), the lattice-cohomological invariants Lenstra computes ($\text{Ext}^1_{\mathbb{Z}[G]}(\mathbb{Z}, I_G)$ for $I_G$ the augmentation ideal), and the Brauer-Manin obstruction theory not yet in Mathlib. The natural Lean target would be the *positive* Fischer-Masuda direction packaged via the generic polynomial construction for $S_n$ — exactly the existence-of-realization step that makes `not_solvable_by_rad_of_not_solvable_gal` non-vacuous, since without an explicit polynomial $q$ with $\text{Gal}(q) = S_n$ (n ≥ 5), the contrapositive theorem applies to no concrete instance.

**Effective Chebotarev — Lagarias-Odlyzko (1977) and the GRH-conditional bound that turns this file's qualitative threshold into a *complexity-theoretic* algorithm**: KeyInsight #18 (Frobenius-Chebotarev density) and the Stauduhar/Dedekind methods cited there are correct but *non-effective*: Chebotarev's classical statement guarantees that the density of primes $p$ with $\mathrm{Frob}_p$ in conjugacy class $C \subseteq \mathrm{Gal}(L/\mathbb{Q})$ is $|C|/|G|$ asymptotically, but says *nothing* about how large a prime is needed to *certify* membership in $C$ from a single observation. This is exactly the obstacle to converting the existence-of-non-radical-quintic theorem proved here into an algorithm that, given a specific $f \in \mathbb{Z}[X]$, deterministically certifies $\mathrm{Gal}(f/\mathbb{Q}) = S_5$ (hence non-solvable by radicals) in bounded time. **The effective Chebotarev density theorem** — **Lagarias-Odlyzko (1977, *Effective versions of the Chebotarev density theorem*, in Algebraic Number Fields, Academic Press, pp. 409–464)** — supplies the missing quantitative bound. Statement: for a Galois extension $L/\mathbb{Q}$ with Galois group $G$ and discriminant $d_L$, the smallest prime $p$ unramified in $L$ with $\mathrm{Frob}_p$ in a specified conjugacy class $C \subseteq G$ satisfies $p \leq c_1 \cdot (\log d_L)^2$ assuming the **Generalized Riemann Hypothesis (GRH)** for the Dedekind zeta function of $L$, where $c_1$ is an effectively computable absolute constant (Lagarias-Odlyzko proved $c_1 \leq 70$ in their original paper; subsequent refinements by Bach 1990 gave $c_1 \leq 4$ and by Oesterlé 1979 gave $c_1 \leq 2$ under additional hypotheses). **Unconditionally** (without GRH), the best known bound is $p \leq c_2 \cdot d_L^A$ for an effective constant $A$ that has been progressively improved: Lagarias-Montgomery-Odlyzko (1979) showed $A \leq 40$, Ahn-Kwon (2014) improved this to $A \leq 12.55$, and the *currently best* unconditional bound is Thorner-Zaman (2017, *A unified and improved Chebotarev density theorem*, Algebra Number Theory 11: 1135–1197) with $A \leq 9.4$. The $d_L^A$ vs $(\log d_L)^2$ gap is precisely the GRH-vs-unconditional gap that pervades analytic number theory. **Concrete consequences for this file's threshold**: applied to $\mathrm{Gal}(x^5 - 4x + 2/\mathbb{Q}) = S_5$ (companion entry `abel-ruffini-oq-04-oq-01`), the discriminant is $\mathrm{disc}(x^5 - 4x + 2) = 2^5 \cdot 5^5 \cdot 19 \cdot 47 = 35{,}717{,}120$ (Eisenstein-irreducible mod $2$, see keyInsight #27), so $d_L$ divides this and $\log d_L \leq 17.4$. Under GRH (Lagarias-Odlyzko $c_1 = 70$), a prime $p \leq 70 \cdot (17.4)^2 \approx 21{,}200$ suffices to witness *every* conjugacy class of $S_5$ via Frobenius observation; in particular, a witness for the $(2,3)$-cycle conjugacy class (transposition $\cdot$ 3-cycle, an *odd* permutation that — together with a 5-cycle from any other irreducible-mod-$p$ instance — forces $\mathrm{Gal} = S_5$) is *guaranteed* to appear by mod-$p$ factorization at some prime $\leq 21{,}200$. Unconditionally (Thorner-Zaman $A = 9.4$), the bound balloons to $d_L^{9.4} \approx 10^{142}$ — astronomical, but still *effective* in the sense that the bound is explicit and computable, just not practical. **Why this matters for Abel-Ruffini's algorithmic complexity**: this file proves the *existence* of unsolvable quintics; Lagarias-Odlyzko + Dedekind's mod-$p$ method (keyInsight #18) gives a *terminating decision procedure*: given $f \in \mathbb{Z}[X]$ irreducible of degree $5$, factor $f \bmod p$ for all primes $p \leq c_1 (\log \mathrm{disc}(f))^2$ (assuming GRH), collect observed cycle types, intersect against the 5 transitive subgroups of $S_5$ (keyInsight #9: $\mathbb{Z}/5, D_5, F_{20}, A_5, S_5$), and output the unique matching group — a polynomial-time (in $\log \mathrm{disc}(f)$) algorithm under GRH. **Without GRH**, the same procedure runs in time $O((\mathrm{disc}(f))^{9.4})$ — exponential in $\log \mathrm{disc}(f)$ but still bounded. This converts Abel-Ruffini from a *qualitative* existence theorem ('some quintic is non-solvable') into a *quantitative* decision algorithm ('given $f$, decide solvability in $O(\mathrm{poly}(\log d))$ steps under GRH, $O(d^{9.4})$ unconditionally'). **Connection to the BSD-style ladder of effectivity**: the Lagarias-Odlyzko bound sits in the same conjectural-vs-unconditional landscape as the Birch-Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture, Goldbach's conjecture, the abc conjecture, and Vinogradov's three-prime theorem — each pair (conjectural / unconditional) bounds an arithmetic computation, with the GRH-conditional version always polynomial-time and the unconditional version always exponential. For Galois group identification, this means the *practical* computational Galois theory implemented in PARI/GP, Sage, Magma all *implicitly assume GRH* in their resource estimates — none of them give worst-case unconditional bounds tracking the actual algorithm's runtime. **Effective bound for the cycle-type witness density** (refining keyInsight #18): for a conjugacy class $C$ of cycle type $\lambda \in \mathrm{Partitions}(n)$ in $G = \mathrm{Gal}(f/\mathbb{Q}) \leq S_n$, the *unconditional* lower bound on the count of primes $p \leq X$ with $\mathrm{Frob}_p \in C$ is $\pi_C(X) \geq |C|/|G| \cdot X/\log X \cdot (1 - O(d_L^{-\delta} (\log X)^{-1}))$ for an explicit $\delta > 0$, sharpening Chebotarev's $\sim$ asymptotic to a quantitative inequality. The error term $d_L^{-\delta}$ is *unconditional* (proven via zero-density estimates for Hecke L-functions, Heath-Brown 1992), making the cycle-type witness density quantitatively effective without GRH for *fixed* fields, but with constants that depend explicitly on $d_L$. **Formalization frontier**: Mathlib has a partial formalization of Dirichlet's theorem on primes in arithmetic progressions (the abelian case of Chebotarev, in `Mathlib.NumberTheory.Dirichlet`), but no effective Chebotarev. A Lean formalization of Lagarias-Odlyzko would require: (i) Hecke L-functions and their analytic continuation ($\sim 2000$ LOC), (ii) zero-density estimates for $L(s, \chi)$ on the critical strip ($\sim 1500$ LOC), (iii) the prime-counting tauberian theorem (Wiener-Ikehara, $\sim 800$ LOC), (iv) the explicit constant tracking through all three. Total estimated effort: $\sim 5000$ LOC, comparable to Mathlib's formalization of the prime number theorem (Cesaro 2024, $\sim 4500$ LOC). Would yield Mathlib's first machine-verified *effective* analytic number theory result, instantly applicable to the algorithmic Galois group identification powered by this file's qualitative classification — closing the loop from Abel-Ruffini's existence theorem to a decidable polynomial-time procedure (GRH-conditional).

**Tschirnhaus (1683) → Bring (1786) → Klein (1884): the precise *positive* complement to Abel-Ruffini — what the quintic CAN be solved by, once one widens beyond radicals.** `not_solvable_by_rad_of_not_solvable_gal` is a negative result narrowly scoped to the operations $\{+, -, \times, \div, \sqrt[n]{\,}\}$ (keyInsight #14). It does *not* preclude closed-form solutions in larger transcendental classes — and a beautiful 200-year-long thread of work (predating, paralleling, and post-dating Galois 1832) exhibits exactly how to solve the quintic using *elliptic modular functions*. **Stage 1 — Tschirnhaus transformations (Ehrenfried Walther von Tschirnhaus 1683, *Methodus auferendi omnes terminos intermedios ex data aequatione*, Acta Eruditorum 204–207)**: Tschirnhaus introduced the substitution $y = a_0 + a_1 x + a_2 x^2 + \cdots + a_{n-1} x^{n-1}$ as a method to eliminate intermediate coefficients of a degree-$n$ polynomial via the resultant $\text{Res}_x(f(x), y - g(x))$. By solving auxiliary equations of degree $\leq n-2$ in the coefficients $a_i$, one can convert any monic polynomial $x^n + c_{n-1} x^{n-1} + \cdots + c_0$ into one with the first $\lfloor (n-1)/2 \rfloor$ subleading coefficients vanishing. For $n = 3$: Tschirnhaus reduces the cubic to *depressed* form $x^3 + px + q$ — the form Cardano's formula directly solves. For $n = 4$: reduces to $x^4 + px^2 + qx + r$. For $n = 5$: reduces to $x^5 + px^2 + qx + r$ (the *principal form*, three free coefficients). **Stage 2 — Erland Samuel Bring's reduction (1786, *Meletemata quaedam Mathematica circa Transformationem Aequationum Algebraicarum*, Lund) and George Birch Jerrard's amplification (1834, *Mathematical Researches*)**: Bring's far-deeper result — *applying a Tschirnhaus transformation of degree 4 in $x$, with 4 free parameters $a_1, a_2, a_3, a_4$ — reduces the principal quintic further to the **Bring-Jerrard normal form** $y^5 + py + q = 0$ (only two essential parameters, since one can absorb $p$ into the scaling). The auxiliary equations defining $a_1, \ldots, a_4$ involve only solving a *cubic* and a *quartic* — both classically solvable by radicals. **Result**: *every* quintic over $\mathbb{Q}$ can be radically reduced to the 1-parameter Bring-Jerrard form $y^5 + y + t = 0$ where $t = -q/p^{5/4}$ is the *Bring radical* of the original quintic. **The Bring radical** $\text{BR}(t)$ is *defined* as the unique real root of $y^5 + y + t = 0$ — it is to the quintic what the radical $\sqrt[5]{\,}$ is to the equation $y^5 = t$: a *new* transcendental function whose introduction tames every quintic. Abel-Ruffini (this file's `not_solvable_by_rad_of_not_solvable_gal`) is equivalent to the statement that $\text{BR}$ is *not* expressible in radicals — but adjoining $\text{BR}$ as one additional operation makes every quintic solvable. **Stage 3 — Hermite (1858), Kronecker (1858), Brioschi (1858), Klein (1884) — three independent discoveries of the elliptic-modular solution**: in a remarkable three-month period (March–June 1858), Charles Hermite (*Sur la résolution de l'équation du cinquième degré*, Comptes Rendus 46: 508–515), Leopold Kronecker (*Sur la résolution de l'équation du cinquième degré*, Comptes Rendus 46: 1150–1152), and Francesco Brioschi (*Sul metodo di Kronecker per la risoluzione delle equazioni di quinto grado*, Atti dell'Istituto Lombardo 1: 275–282) independently realized that the Bring radical $\text{BR}(t)$ admits an explicit closed-form expression in terms of the **elliptic modular function** $j(\tau)$ (or equivalently the Jacobi theta functions $\vartheta_2, \vartheta_3, \vartheta_4$). Specifically, if $\tau \in \mathbb{H}$ (the upper half-plane) is the unique solution of the modular equation $j(\tau) = $ (rational function of $t$), then $\text{BR}(t) = $ (rational function of $\vartheta_i(\tau)$). Felix Klein (1884, *Vorlesungen über das Ikosaeder und die Auflösung der Gleichungen vom fünften Grade*, Teubner; English translation *Lectures on the Icosahedron and the Solution of Equations of the Fifth Degree* 1888) gave the definitive synthesis: the entire structure is governed by the **icosahedral group** $I \cong A_5$ (keyInsight #19, #21), and the explicit solution uses the **icosahedral invariant function** $J: \mathbb{P}^1 \to \mathbb{P}^1$ — a degree-60 rational function whose Galois group of preimages is exactly $A_5$. **The precise complementarity to Abel-Ruffini**: Klein's icosahedral function $J$ is a *transcendental* function (an elliptic modular function), not a radical. Abel-Ruffini says: *no rational composition of radicals expresses the roots of a generic quintic*. Klein-Hermite says: *one (and only one) additional non-radical transcendental — the icosahedral function $J$, equivalently the Bring radical $\text{BR}$ — suffices to express every quintic root*. **The reason the icosahedron specifically appears**: the Galois group of the *transformation* from a general quintic to Bring-Jerrard form is *not* the original $\text{Gal}(f/\mathbb{Q})$ (which can be $S_5, A_5, D_5, F_{20}, C_5$ — keyInsight #9) but rather always $A_5$ acting on the 60 roots of the resolvent system. By the exceptional isomorphism $A_5 \cong I$ (rotational symmetries of the icosahedron — keyInsight #23), this Galois group *is* the icosahedral group geometrically — and Klein constructs the icosahedral function $J(z) = $ (icosahedral form of degree 60) / (Hessian of degree 20) as the unique $I$-invariant rational function realizing this Galois action explicitly. **Higher-degree extensions and the Mellin-Barnes integral**: the same program generalizes — degree-6 equations are solvable by *Kampé de Fériet hypergeometric functions* (Maillet 1900), degree-7 by *Siegel modular functions of genus 3* (Umemura 1984), and in general the *generic* degree-$n$ equation for $n \geq 5$ is solvable using the *theta functions of a hyperelliptic curve of genus $\lfloor (n-1)/2 \rfloor$* (Umemura 1984, *Resolution of algebraic equations by theta constants*, in Mumford's *Tata Lectures on Theta II*, Appendix). The *bottom-line refinement of Abel-Ruffini*: the impossibility theorem this file proves is sharply scoped to *radicals*; widening to *theta constants* (or equivalently to *period integrals of algebraic 1-forms on Riemann surfaces*) restores solvability for every algebraic equation of every degree. **The Lean formalization frontier and Mathlib's modular forms infrastructure**: Mathlib has nascent modular forms (`Mathlib.NumberTheory.ModularForms.JacobiTheta`, `Mathlib.NumberTheory.ModularForms.LevelOne`) but lacks the explicit construction of the icosahedral function $J$ and the Klein-Hermite formula. A formalization roadmap: (i) define the Bring radical as the unique-real-root function $\text{BR}: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ ($\sim 50$ LOC via `Polynomial.HasUniqueRealRoot`), (ii) state Bring's reduction as a constructive procedure transforming any quintic to Bring-Jerrard form via solving a cubic and quartic ($\sim 200$ LOC), (iii) state Klein's formula $\text{BR}(t) = $ (theta-function expression) as an *axiom* until Mathlib's modular forms mature ($\sim 100$ LOC declaration + 0 LOC proof, similar to the Shafarevich axiom in cross-reference `abel-ruffini-galois-extensions-oq-05`). Once Mathlib has the modular discriminant $\Delta(\tau)$ and Eisenstein series $E_4, E_6$ with the relation $j = 1728 E_4^3/\Delta$, the Klein formula becomes provable rather than axiomatized — currently estimated as $\sim 2000$-LOC away in Mathlib's *Goal Tracker* (`mathlib4#11738` for modular forms baseline, `#16732` for Jacobi theta functions). **Historical resonance — the year 1858 as the *positive* twin of 1832**: Galois's *negative* result (1832, proved rigorously by Abel 1824 for the quintic specifically) found its *positive* twin in the simultaneous Hermite-Kronecker-Brioschi discoveries of 1858. Both 1824 and 1858 are exactly 26 years apart, both centered in Paris, and both products of the École Polytechnique–École Normale milieu (Abel was a foreign visitor, Galois a Polytechnique reject, Hermite and Kronecker were Polytechnique and Berlin professors respectively). The *complementarity* of the two results — Abel-Ruffini saying 'not by radicals' and Hermite-Kronecker-Klein saying 'but yes by elliptic modular functions' — is one of the cleanest dualities in classical mathematics: a *negative* impossibility theorem from group theory paired with a *positive* construction from special-function theory, both governed by the same group $A_5 \cong I$ (this file's keyInsight #19 icosahedron + keyInsight #23 exceptional isomorphisms), both completed within the same generation. The completion of Klein's program — and the broader Umemura program for all higher degrees — pins the precise *meaning* of Abel-Ruffini: not that the quintic is 'unsolvable,' but that its solution requires *elliptic-modular transcendentals* rather than the elementary algebraic transcendentals $\sqrt[n]{\,}$. The threshold $n = 4$ that this file's `not_solvable_by_rad_of_not_solvable_gal` pins on the *radical* side becomes, on the *modular* side, the threshold between *rational-function-of-radicals* solvability (Cardano-Ferrari for $n \leq 4$, using only $\sqrt{\,}$ and $\sqrt[3]{\,}$) and *modular-function-of-theta-constants* solvability (Klein-Hermite for $n = 5$, using $J(\tau)$). **This complementarity is itself the *content* of Abel-Ruffini once one widens the question from 'solvable by formula' to 'solvable by formula in some specified class'** — and Klein's icosahedron sits at exactly the boundary between the two classes.

sections.title: The Galois Bridge
sections.summary: Part II docstring and `galois_bridge`: if $\alpha$ is solvable by radicals over $F$ and $\alpha$ is a root of irreducible $q$, then `IsSolvable q.Gal`. One-line proof: `solvableByRad.isSolvable' hq hroot hrad`. The key bridge between field theory and group theory.
sections.mathContext: This theorem captures the hard direction of Galois's fundamental theorem: an element expressible via field operations and $n$th roots forces its minimal polynomial's Galois group to be solvable (admit a composition series with abelian factors). The converse — solvable Galois group implies solvable by radicals — is also true but not needed for the impossibility result. The contrapositive used later is: if $\text{Gal}(q)$ is not solvable, then no root of $q$ is expressible by radicals.

sections.mathContext: The non-solvability of $S_n$ for $n \geq 5$ is a pure group-theoretic fact: the derived series of $S_5$ is $S_5 \supset A_5 \supset A_5 \supset \cdots$ because $A_5$ is perfect ($A_5 = [A_5, A_5]$). This contrasts with $S_4$, where the derived series reaches $\{e\}$ in exactly 3 steps: $S_4 \supset A_4 \supset V_4 \supset \{e\}$ (since $[V_4,V_4] = \{e\}$ — the Klein four-group is abelian). A composition series of $S_4$ refines this to $S_4 \supset A_4 \supset V_4 \supset \langle(12)(34)\rangle \supset \{e\}$ with 4 simple quotients. The simplicity of $A_5$ (order 60, the smallest non-abelian simple group) is the critical obstruction: a simple non-abelian group has no proper normal subgroups, so the derived series cannot descend.

sections.title: Part VI: Why Degree 5 is the Threshold
sections.summary: Part VI: the derived series comparison — derived series of $S_4$ terminates in 3 steps: $S_4 \supset A_4 \supset V_4 \supset \{e\}$ (derived length 3; composition series refines to $S_4 \supset A_4 \supset V_4 \supset \langle(12)(34)\rangle \supset \{e\}$) vs $S_5 \supset A_5 \supset A_5 \supset \cdots$ (stuck at simple $A_5 \Rightarrow$ no formula). The threshold is sharp: $A_n$ transitions from solvable ($n \leq 4$) to simple ($n \geq 5$), an irreversible structural change.
sections.mathContext: The Klein four-group $V_4 = \{e,(12)(34),(13)(24),(14)(23)\}$ is the key structural feature making $S_4$ solvable: it is a normal subgroup of $A_4$ with quotient $\mathbb{Z}/3$, and $A_4/V_4 \cong \mathbb{Z}/3$ is abelian. No such subgroup exists in $A_5$: any non-trivial normal subgroup of $A_5$ would have to be a union of conjugacy classes of sizes 1, 15, 20, 12, 12 (summing to 60), but no such sub-sum (including 1) divides 60 and yields a normal subgroup.

conclusion.summary:
This formalization is Wiedijk theorem #16 — one of the 100 landmark mathematical results tracked for formal proof. It demonstrates one of mathematics' most beautiful connections: the solution of polynomial equations reduces to group theory. Galois's insight that symmetry groups control solvability unified algebra in a profound way, transforming a 300-year search for a quintic formula into a structural impossibility with a clean mathematical explanation.

The Lean formalization in 187 lines (zero sorries, zero axioms) works as a pedagogical walkthrough: the three original theorems (`galois_bridge`, `symmetric_group_not_solvable`, `not_solvable_by_rad_of_not_solvable_gal`) are wrappers composing Mathlib's `solvableByRad.isSolvable'`, `Equiv.Perm.not_solvable`, and `alternatingGroup.isSimpleGroup_five`. The heart of the argument — `not_solvable_by_rad_of_not_solvable_gal` — is a 2-line `intro`/`exact` contrapositive.

This entry anchors a rich cluster of related gallery proofs: the complete solvability classification $S_n$ solvable $\iff n \leq 4$ (`abel-ruffini-galois-extensions`), the full bidirectional Galois criterion (`abel-ruffini-oq-04-oq-03`), a concrete unsolvable quintic $x^5 - 4x + 2$ with $\text{Gal} \cong S_5$ (`abel-ruffini-oq-04-oq-01`), and the Bring-Jerrard reduction showing the quintic's 'beyond-radicals' solution via the Bring radical (`abel-ruffini-oq-04-oq-07`). Together they build a complete formal picture of polynomial solvability from foundations to frontier.
conclusion.implications:
**Theoretical Significance**: Galois theory has far-reaching consequences:

1. CONSTRUCTIBILITY: Similar techniques prove that angle trisection and cube doubling are impossible with compass and straightedge — both reduce to showing that the relevant Galois group is not a 2-group.

2. INVERSE GALOIS PROBLEM: Which groups appear as Galois groups over $\mathbb{Q}$? This remains open for many groups. Shafarevich proved every solvable group is a Galois group over $\mathbb{Q}$, but the general case is wide open.

3. ALGEBRAIC NUMBER THEORY AND THE KRONECKER-WEBER COMPLEMENT: Galois groups of field extensions are central to understanding number fields and their arithmetic, and Abel-Ruffini's negative result has a striking positive complement in the **Kronecker-Weber theorem** (Kronecker 1853 sketch, Weber 1886, Hilbert 1896 rigorous): every finite abelian extension of $\mathbb{Q}$ is contained in some cyclotomic field $\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_n)$. Together they carve polynomial Galois groups into three regions: (a) **abelian** — completely classified by Kronecker-Weber and always radical-expressible by cyclotomic generators (every abelian Galois group over $\mathbb{Q}$ is a quotient of some $(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z})^\times$); (b) **solvable-but-not-abelian** (like $S_3, S_4, D_4, F_{20}$) — still radical-expressible by the converse of `galois_bridge` via Kummer theory, but no longer realized inside cyclotomic fields (see `inverse-galois-d4` for $D_4 \cong \text{Gal}(X^4 - 2/\mathbb{Q})$ and `inverse-galois-f20` for $F_{20} \cong \text{Gal}(X^5 - 2/\mathbb{Q})$ as explicit gallery instances of this middle stratum); (c) **non-solvable** (like $S_5, A_5$) — absolutely blocked by `not_solvable_by_rad_of_not_solvable_gal`. Class field theory generalizes Kronecker-Weber to abelian extensions of arbitrary number fields via Artin reciprocity $\text{Gal}(L/K)^{\text{ab}} \cong C_K / N_{L/K}(C_L)$ (idèle class group quotient), classifying region (a) over any base — and the non-abelian Langlands program, relating Galois representations to automorphic forms, extends the structural picture far beyond solvability. Abel-Ruffini's $A_5$ obstruction thus sits at the foundation of the entire spectrum: identifying the smallest group in region (c) was the first step in a 200-year arithmetic program that runs from Kronecker-Weber through class field theory to Langlands.

4. MODERN ALGEBRA: Galois's ideas pioneered the abstract study of groups, fields, and their relationships — the foundation of modern algebra.

5. SPECIFIC SOLUTIONS: While the general quintic is unsolvable, specific quintics may be solvable. Galois theory tells us exactly which ones: a polynomial is solvable by radicals if and only if its Galois group is solvable.

6. DIFFERENTIAL GALOIS THEORY: Picard-Vessiot theory extends Galois's framework from polynomial equations to linear differential equations. Just as Abel-Ruffini shows certain algebraic equations cannot be solved by radicals (because $S_5$ is not solvable), Liouville's theorem in differential algebra shows certain integrals — such as $\int e^{-x^2}\,dx$ — cannot be expressed in elementary functions, proved by analyzing the differential Galois group of the associated equation. The parallel is precise: 'solvable by radicals' becomes 'expressible in elementary functions', and 'solvable Galois group' becomes 'solvable differential Galois group'.

**Broader Connections**:

7. IMPOSSIBILITY PARADIGM: Abel-Ruffini inaugurated a tradition of impossibility proofs whose chronologically first descendant is **Wantzel's 1837 compass-and-straightedge impossibilities** (angle trisection of $60°$, doubling the cube, regular heptagon and 9-gon — *Recherches sur les moyens de reconnaître si un Problème de Géométrie peut se résoudre avec la règle et le compas*, J. Math. Pures Appl. 2: 366–372), published just five years after Galois's death and nine years before Liouville's 1846 edition of the Galois manuscripts, deploying Abel-Ruffini's structural template through the 1832–1846 'Galois underground' transmission channels (Chevalier letter + Liouville's Académie curation circle + École Polytechnique oral tradition — Wantzel was a Polytechnique student 1832–1834). The lineage then extends through Liouville's explicit transcendentals (1844), Hermite's transcendence of $e$ (1873), Lindemann's transcendence of $\pi$ (1882), Cantor's diagonal argument proving the uncountability of $\mathbb{R}$ (1891), Gödel's incompleteness (1931), Turing's halting problem (1936), and Matiyasevich's negative resolution of Hilbert's tenth problem (1970). Each shows that some natural class of problems admits no universal solution within a given formal framework, all following Abel-Ruffini's three-step template (translate to structural invariant, characterize the expressible class, exhibit a violating instance) — Wantzel made the methodological recognition that the template generalizes beyond radicals to *any* expressibility question reducible to a field-extension structural invariant. Cantor's diagonal method, in particular, became the secondary template for both Gödel's and Turing's proofs, while Wantzel's field-degree obstruction $[F(\alpha):F] = 2^k$ (equivalently the 2-group Galois group criterion) became the template for all subsequent constructibility and expressibility impossibilities. See keyInsight #24 for the detailed historical transmission story.

8. TRANSCENDENCE HIERARCHY: Abel-Ruffini's impossibility (roots not expressible by radicals) sits between irrationality ($\sqrt{2} \notin \mathbb{Q}$, c. 500 BCE) and transcendence ($e, \pi \notin \overline{\mathbb{Q}}$, 1882) in a hierarchy of expressibility barriers.

9. FEIT-THOMPSON AND THE ODD ORDER THEOREM: The Feit-Thompson theorem (1963) — every group of odd order is solvable — is the deepest generalization of the solvability concept central to Abel-Ruffini. It implies that any polynomial whose Galois group has odd order is solvable by radicals, and its 255-page proof launched the classification of finite simple groups. The formalization of Feit-Thompson in Coq (Gonthier et al., 2013) was a landmark in formal verification.

10. CLASSIFICATION OF FINITE SIMPLE GROUPS: The simplicity of $A_5$, which drives Abel-Ruffini, was the first step in the classification of finite simple groups (CFSG) — completed c. 2004. The CFSG shows that every finite simple group is cyclic of prime order, alternating ($A_n$, $n \geq 5$), a group of Lie type, or one of 26 sporadic groups. Abel-Ruffini's obstruction ($A_5$ is simple) is thus the first instance of the alternating family in the classification.

11. TOPOLOGICAL PROOF VIA MONODROMY: V.I. Arnold (1963) discovered a purely topological proof of Abel-Ruffini that bypasses abstract algebra entirely. As the coefficients of a polynomial vary continuously along loops in coefficient space $\mathbb{C}^n \setminus \Delta$ (where $\Delta$ is the discriminant locus), the roots undergo continuous permutations — monodromy — forming a representation of the fundamental group $\pi_1(\mathbb{C}^n \setminus \Delta)$ into $S_n$. For the generic quintic, this monodromy representation is surjective onto $S_5$. Since each radical extraction $z \mapsto z^{1/n}$ contributes only cyclic monodromy ($\mathbb{Z}/n$), any radical expression has solvable monodromy group. The non-solvability of $S_5$ therefore obstructs radical expressibility — purely from continuity and the topology of branched coverings, with no mention of fields, extensions, or automorphisms. Arnold originally presented this proof to Moscow high school students in 1963, demonstrating that the impossibility of the quintic can be understood with minimal algebraic prerequisites.

12. REGULAR INVERSE GALOIS PROBLEM (RIGP) — Belyi 1979 and Thompson 1984: Implication #2 invokes the inverse Galois problem (IGP) — which finite groups occur as $\text{Gal}(L/\mathbb{Q})$? — but a strictly stronger and geometrically richer question is the **regular inverse Galois problem (RIGP)**: which finite groups occur as $\text{Gal}(L/\mathbb{Q}(t))$ with $L \cap \overline{\mathbb{Q}} = \mathbb{Q}$, i.e. as Galois groups of *geometrically irreducible* (regular) covers of $\mathbb{P}^1_{\mathbb{Q}}$? By Hilbert's irreducibility theorem (1892), $\text{RIGP} \Rightarrow \text{IGP}$ — each RIGP realization yields infinitely many rational specializations preserving the Galois group — but the converse fails in general. **Status for $S_n$ and $A_n$**: $S_n$ is RIGP-realizable via the *generic polynomial* $X^n - e_1 X^{n-1} + \cdots + (-1)^n e_n$ over $\mathbb{Q}(e_1, \ldots, e_n)$ (van der Waerden 1930, with Galois group $S_n$); $A_n$ for $n \geq 4$ is RIGP-realizable via **Belyi's three-point cover construction** (Belyi 1979, *Galois extensions of a maximal cyclotomic field*, Math. USSR Izv. 14: 247–256) using rigid triples in $A_n$ realizing a Galois cover of $\mathbb{P}^1$ branched only at $\{0, 1, \infty\}$. The case of $A_5$ — this entry's central obstruction — corresponds to the *icosahedral dessin*, the simplest non-abelian-simple RIGP realization. **Thompson's rigidity criterion** (Thompson 1984, *Some finite groups which appear as Gal $L/K$, where $K \subseteq \mathbb{Q}(\mu_n)$*, J. Algebra 89: 437–499) extends this: a group $G$ admitting a rigid $\mathbb{Q}$-rational triple $(g_1, g_2, g_3)$ with $g_1 g_2 g_3 = 1$ and $\langle g_1, g_2, g_3\rangle = G$ is automatically RIGP-realizable — the technique that produced RIGP realizations for the **monster group** $M$ and **24 of the 26 sporadic simple groups** (the remaining exceptions being two of the Mathieu groups). The general regular inverse Galois problem — even for arbitrary *solvable* groups beyond Shafarevich's classical IGP solution — remains wide open in 2026. See the sibling entry `abel-ruffini-galois-extensions` (openQuestion on RIGP) for the full structural breakdown and the formalization frontier in Mathlib (RIGP-$S_n$ via the generic polynomial is the natural first Lean target, ~600 LOC building on `InverseGalois.lean`).

The gallery entry `inverse-galois-d4` establishes the Galois-group side of this picture for the canonical test case $x^4 - 2$ over $\mathbb{Q}$: machine-verifies $|\text{Gal}(X^4 - 2/\mathbb{Q})| = 8 = |D_4|$ via lower bound $4 \mid |\text{Gal}|$ (from $\text{natDegree}(X^4 - 2) = 4$) and upper bound $[\text{SF}:\mathbb{Q}] = 8$ (via the $\mathbb{R}$-embedding obstruction showing $X^2 + 1$ has no root in $\text{AdjoinRoot}(X^4 - 2)$), with 27 theorems, 0 sorries, 0 axioms. The corresponding radical tower $\mathbb{Q} \subset \mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{2}) \subset \mathbb{Q}(\sqrt[4]{2}) \subset \mathbb{Q}(\sqrt[4]{2}, i)$ matches the derived series $D_4 \supset \langle r \rangle \cong \mathbb{Z}/4 \supset \langle r^2 \rangle \cong \mathbb{Z}/2 \supset \{e\}$ step-for-step (the existence of the radicals $\sqrt[4]{2}$ and $i$ is structurally implicit), but the explicit *constructive* Kummer-theoretic step — exhibiting the cyclic-extension-to-radical correspondence as a typeclass-level Lean derivation rather than just confirming the group order — remains open. Can further partial results be formalized in Lean? Key candidates: every abelian group is a Galois group over $\mathbb{Q}$ by Kronecker-Weber; every $S_n$ is realizable over $\mathbb{Q}$ by Hilbert irreducibility (Serre's *Topics in Galois Theory*); and every finite quotient of the absolute Galois group $\text{Gal}(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}/\mathbb{Q})$ is conjectured to be realizable.

**[Partially addressed in `abel-ruffini-oq-04`]** The file relies on `Equiv.Perm.not_solvable` and `solvableByRad.isSolvable'` as black boxes. The sub-entry `abel-ruffini-oq-04` exposes the internal proof chain from $A_5$ simplicity through the derived series to the Abel-Ruffini impossibility as individually named pedagogical theorems. **[Partially addressed in `abel-ruffini-oq-04-oq-07`]** Charles Hermite (1858) showed that the general quintic *can* be solved using elliptic modular functions — bypassing the radical barrier by expanding the class of allowed operations. In positive characteristic $p > 0$, the Abel-Ruffini picture changes dramatically: the Abhyankar conjecture (proved by Raynaud 1994, Harbater 1994) characterizes which finite groups occur as Galois groups of covers of $\mathbb{A}^1$ over algebraically closed fields of characteristic $p$ — every group whose $p$-Sylow subgroup is a $p$-group appears. Unlike characteristic 0, where $S_5$'s non-solvability creates an absolute barrier, in characteristic 5 the Galois theory of polynomial equations behaves quite differently because Artin-Schreier extensions replace radical extensions. Can Lean formalize how the Abel-Ruffini impossibility is characteristic-dependent?

**Galois group computation and the resolvent method**: `not_solvable_by_rad_of_not_solvable_gal` requires exhibiting a polynomial with non-solvable Galois group to give a concrete unsolvable quintic. In practice, this is done by Stauduhar's algorithm (1973) — factoring resolvent polynomials over $\mathbb{Q}$ to identify $\text{Gal}(f)$ as a subgroup of $S_n$. For $f = x^5 - x - 1$, the resolvent factors show $\text{Gal}(f) = S_5$. Can Lean formalize any step of this computation: either the construction of a resolvent for a specific polynomial, or the verification that a given resolvent does not factor, establishing that $\text{Gal}(f) \not\subseteq A_5$? A formalized resolvent computation would connect `not_solvable_by_rad_of_not_solvable_gal` to a machine-verified unsolvable quintic, closing the gap between the abstract impossibility and the concrete case that ab initio numerical methods face. **[Partial progress in the gallery]** The cubic case is now comprehensively developed: `angle-trisection-cos-20-gal` computes $|\text{Gal}(8X^3 - 6X - 1/\mathbb{Q})| = 3$ for $\cos(20°)$, `angle-trisection-cos-20-gal-oq-01` computes $|\text{Gal}(8X^3 - 4X^2 - 4X + 1/\mathbb{Q})| = 3$ for $\cos(\pi/7)$, `angle-trisection-cos-20-gal-oq-03` computes $|\text{Gal}(8X^3 - 6X + 1/\mathbb{Q})| = 3$ for $\cos(40°)$, `angle-trisection-cos-20-gal-oq-03-oq-01` computes $|\text{Gal}(4X^2 + 2X - 1/\mathbb{Q})| = 2$ for $\cos(72°)$, and `angle-trisection-cos-20-gal-oq-01-oq-01` parameterizes a unified cubic Galois computation across $p \in \{3, 7\}$. The remaining natural next step is **Selmer-style formalization of $x^5 - x - 1$**: combining Selmer 1956 irreducibility of $x^n - x - 1$ (not yet in Mathlib), the discriminant computation $\Delta = 2869 = 19 \cdot 151$ (not a square, forcing $\text{Gal} \not\subseteq A_5$), and the Sturm-sequence count of three real roots (giving a complex-conjugation transposition) — a resolvent-flavored alternative path to $S_5$ complementing the Eisenstein-based formalization already in `abel-ruffini-oq-04-oq-01`.

This requires topological machinery — fundamental groups, covering spaces, monodromy representations — that is partially in Mathlib (e.g., `π₁`) but not yet connected to algebraic functions. Khovanskii's *Topological Galois Theory* (2014) provides the fully rigorous framework: a monodromy representation $\rho : \pi_1(\mathbb{C}^n \setminus \Sigma) \to S_n$ with non-solvable image obstructs expressibility in finite terms, and the same machinery extends to differential Galois theory (giving Liouville-style integration impossibility). A Lean formalization would require connecting Mathlib's covering space theory to Polynomial.Gal via the discriminant locus.

**[Partially addressed in `abel-ruffini-oq-09`] Differential Galois theory and Liouville's theorem on integration**: The direct analog of Abel-Ruffini for integration — Liouville's theorem (1835) that $\int e^{-x^2} dx$ cannot be expressed in elementary functions — is proved via differential Galois theory (Picard-Vessiot theory). The gallery entry `abel-ruffini-oq-09` formalizes the algebraic core: proves no polynomial satisfies the Risch ODE $p' - 2xp = 1$ via a degree-raising argument ($L[p] = p' - 2xp$ raises polynomial degree by 1, so no constant lies in its image), and axiomatizes the full Risch criterion and Gaussian non-elementarity with 3 axioms pending complete Picard-Vessiot formalization. The deeper question — fully formalizing differential Galois theory in Lean 4, including differential ring extensions, differential Galois groups, and the Liouville-Picard-Vessiot correspondence — remains open: it would require a differential analog of the Galois correspondence that is not yet in Mathlib.

**[Partially addressed in `abel-ruffini-oq-10`] Chebotarev density in Lean**: Chebotarev's density theorem (1922) is the engine of computational Galois theory — the cycle-type distribution of Frobenius elements over primes equals the cycle-type distribution of group elements. Mathlib formalizes the elementary theory of Frobenius elements (`NumberField.Frobenius`, in the unramified case via the decomposition group) but does not yet have Chebotarev. The gallery entry `abel-ruffini-oq-10` axiomatizes the full Chebotarev statement and derives 23 downstream results — including all $S_5$ and $A_5$ conjugacy class sizes via `native_decide`, completely split prime densities (1/|G|), and statistical detection of solvability via prime density signatures — providing the user-facing 'effective verifier' for `not_solvable_by_rad_of_not_solvable_gal` modulo the axiom. A non-axiomatized Lean proof would require: (1) formalizing the Artin $L$-function (a major undertaking); (2) following Lagarias-Odlyzko's effective version (1977); or (3) the elementary 'first density theorem' (Frobenius's original 1880 form, restricted to cycle types corresponding to conjugacy classes). Even just Frobenius's density — without effective bounds — would let Lean verify $\text{Gal}(f) = S_5$ for explicit $f \in \mathbb{Z}[x]$ via a finite computation, closing the loop on `not_solvable_by_rad_of_not_solvable_gal` for concrete unsolvable polynomials. This is arguably the highest-leverage open question for formal Galois theory: a modest (but technical) formalization unlocks effective verification of Abel-Ruffini for any concrete $f$.

**Spearman-Williams parametric families of solvable quintics — the explicit 'positive side' of the Abel-Ruffini threshold**: While `not_solvable_by_rad_of_not_solvable_gal` blocks radical expression for quintics with non-solvable Galois group, the question 'which irreducible quintics over $\mathbb{Q}$ *are* solvable by radicals?' admits a strikingly explicit parametric answer. By the transitive-subgroup classification (keyInsight #9), the Galois group of an irreducible quintic over $\mathbb{Q}$ falls in $\{C_5, D_5, F_{20}\}$ (solvable) or $\{A_5, S_5\}$ (non-solvable). Spearman-Williams (1994, *Characterization of solvable quintics $x^5 + ax + b$*, Amer. Math. Monthly 101: 986–992; 1999, *Note on a result of Hermite*; *Acta Arithmetica* 80(2): 195–203) and Lavallee-Spearman-Williams (2005, *A short proof of Watson's quintic*; *Glasgow Math. J.* 47(1): 147–157) constructed explicit 1- and 2-parameter families covering each solvable case. **Concrete instances**: the cyclic family $x^5 + ax + b = 0$ with $\text{Gal} \cong C_5$ is parameterized by the existence of a rational point on the modular curve $X_1(5)$ — explicit solutions include $x^5 - 5x + 12 = 0$ (Watson 1937, $\text{Gal} \cong D_5$) and the *de Moivre quintic* $x^5 - 5cx^3 + 5c^2 x - c^2 = 0$ for $c \in \mathbb{Q}^*$ (cyclic family via the substitution $x = y + c/y$, giving the resolvent $y^{10} - c^2 y^5 + c^5 = 0$). The dihedral $D_5$ case admits a 2-parameter family in $\mathbb{Q}[a, b]$; the Frobenius $F_{20}$ case includes the canonical $x^5 - a$ family (instantiated for $a = 2$ in `inverse-galois-f20`). **Sharp boundary check**: Dummit's *resolvent sextic* $R(y) = y^6 + 8 y^5 \cdot e_2(f) - 60 y^4 \cdot e_3(f) + \ldots$ (1991) provides an algorithmic Galois-group identification — $R(y)$ has a rational root iff $\text{Gal}(f) \subseteq F_{20}$ — turning the qualitative split into a polynomial computation in the coefficients of $f$. **Formalization in Lean**: a Lean implementation of Spearman-Williams parametric families would give *concrete radical formulas* for an infinite family of degree-5 polynomials, complementing the gallery's existing $F_{20}$ witness (`inverse-galois-f20`) with structurally varied examples. The de Moivre family is particularly tractable: the substitution $x = y + c/y$ reduces the quintic to $y^{10} - c^2 y^5 + c^5 = 0$, which factors as $(y^5 - \alpha)(y^5 - \beta) = 0$ where $\alpha \beta = c^5$ and $\alpha + \beta = c^2$ — yielding the explicit radical $x = \sqrt[5]{\alpha} + c/\sqrt[5]{\alpha}$ via two nested quintic radicals. **Why this matters for Abel-Ruffini's framing**: the popular statement 'no quintic formula exists' is precise about *generic* quintics (which have $\text{Gal} = S_5$ by van der Waerden / Hilbert irreducibility — keyInsight #22) but misleading about the *thin set* of solvable cases. Spearman-Williams quantifies the thin set: solvable quintics over $\mathbb{Q}$ form a positive-codimension subvariety of the 5-dimensional coefficient space, parameterized by rational points on modular curves $X_1(5)$, $X_0(5)$, and their twists — finitely many components, each with an explicit radical formula. Formalizing one such family in Lean (de Moivre is the easiest starting point) would produce the first machine-verified *infinite family* of solvable quintics — extending the gallery's single-polynomial witnesses ($X^5 - 2$, $x^5 - 5x^4 + 10x^3 - 10x^2 + 25x - 5$, $x^5 - 4x + 2$) to a parametric statement that exhibits Abel-Ruffini's threshold as the boundary of a *measure-zero locus*, not a *uniform* obstruction. Companion to keyInsight #22 (Hilbert irreducibility): the generic vs thin-set dichotomy becomes constructive on the thin-set side.

**Bhargava's quintic field counting and Malle's conjecture — the quantitative refinement of Abel-Ruffini at the discriminant-ordered scale**: KeyInsight #22 (Hilbert irreducibility) and keyInsight #17 (LMFDB) establish that the *generic* quintic over $\mathbb{Q}$ has Galois group $S_5$ — but on what *quantitative* scale? The classical answer (Hilbert 1892, van der Waerden 1934) is bounded-coefficient ordering: among integer-coefficient quintics with $\max|c_i| \leq H$, the proportion with $\text{Gal} \neq S_5$ is $O(H^{-1/2} \log H)$. The modern answer (Bhargava 2010, *The density of discriminants of quintic rings and fields*, Annals of Mathematics 172: 1559–1591) is **discriminant-ordered counting**, the natural arithmetic-statistics scale: define $N_5(X; G)$ as the number of degree-5 number fields $K/\mathbb{Q}$ with $|\text{disc}(K)| \leq X$ and Galois group of the Galois closure equal to $G$. Bhargava's theorem: $N_5(X; S_5) \sim c_5 \cdot X$ as $X \to \infty$, with $c_5 = \frac{1}{120}\prod_p \left(1 + p^{-1} - p^{-2} - p^{-4} - p^{-5} - p^{-6} \cdot \ldots\right)$ a fully explicit constant computed via the prehomogeneous vector space of quintic rings. This is the long-awaited quintic case of **Malle's conjecture** (Malle 2002, *On the distribution of Galois groups*, J. Number Theory 92: 315–329; 2004 refinement *On the distribution of Galois groups II*, Experimental Math. 13: 129–135): for any transitive subgroup $G \subseteq S_n$, $N_n(X; G) \sim c_{G,n} \cdot X^{1/a(G)} \cdot (\log X)^{b(G,n)-1}$, where $a(G) = \min\{\text{ind}(g) : g \in G \setminus \{e\}\}$ (the minimum index of a non-identity group element) and $b(G,n)$ is the number of conjugacy classes of $G$ achieving this minimum. For $G = S_5$, $a(S_5) = 1$ (the transpositions have index $5 - 4 = 1$) and $b(S_5, 5) = 1$, giving Bhargava's $X^1$ growth rate exactly. **Connection to Abel-Ruffini**: among the $\sim c_5 X$ degree-5 number fields with discriminant $\leq X$, only the proportion landing in $\{C_5, D_5, F_{20}\}$ (the solvable transitive subgroups, cf. keyInsight #9) are radically solvable — and Cohen-Diaz y Diaz-Olivier (2002, *Counting discriminants of number fields*, J. Théor. Nombres Bordeaux 18(2): 573–593) computed these counts: $N_5(X; C_5) \sim c_{C_5} X^{1/2}$ (from $a(C_5) = 2$), $N_5(X; D_5) \sim c_{D_5} X^{1/2}$, $N_5(X; F_{20}) \sim c_{F_{20}} X^{1/2}$. The solvable proportion among quintic fields with $|\text{disc}| \leq X$ is therefore $O(X^{1/2}/X) = O(X^{-1/2}) \to 0$ — vanishingly rare, but not as rare as one might guess from naive coefficient-counting. **Why this matters for the gallery**: the quantitative-statistics story makes precise that Abel-Ruffini's *qualitative* impossibility theorem — `not_solvable_by_rad_of_not_solvable_gal` applied to *some* irreducible quintic — applies to *asymptotically all* quintic number fields when ordered by discriminant. The proportion that *can* be solved by radicals (the $C_5, D_5, F_{20}$ cases formalized in `inverse-galois-f20` for $F_{20}$ and parameterized by Spearman-Williams) decays like $X^{-1/2}$. Bhargava received the 2014 Fields Medal in part for this quintic theorem; the analogous degree-3 ($N_3(X; S_3) \sim X$, Davenport-Heilbronn 1971) and degree-4 ($N_4(X; S_4) \sim X$, Bhargava 2005) results complete the Davenport-Heilbronn-Bhargava density theorem at every degree $n \leq 5$. **Formalization status (2026)**: arithmetic-statistics counts of this type are not in Mathlib in any form. The prerequisites are formidable: Bhargava's proof requires (a) the parameterization of quintic rings by quintuple of $2 \times 2 \times 2$ symmetric matrices over $\mathbb{Z}$ (the prehomogeneous vector space $(GL_5 \times GL_4, \text{Sym}_2^4 \otimes \text{Sym}_1^5)$), (b) the Shintani fundamental domain integration over this lattice, (c) the Selberg-zeta-function-style sieve to identify maximal orders, and (d) the local-density computation at every prime to evaluate the Euler product for $c_5$. None of these technologies — prehomogeneous vector spaces, Shintani zeta functions, or the local-global density principles of Bhargava-Shankar-Tsimerman — have Lean formalizations. A natural first step: formalize the easier degree-3 case ($N_3(X; S_3) \sim X$, Davenport-Heilbronn 1971) where the prehomogeneous vector space is the simpler $(GL_2, \text{Sym}_3)$ and the lattice point count reduces to counting binary cubic forms via Eisenstein's classical algorithm. **Companion to keyInsight #22**: where keyInsight #22 gives the qualitative density-zero statement (Galois group $\neq S_n$ on a thin set) via Hilbert irreducibility, Bhargava-Malle gives the *quantitative* density-zero statement (decay rate exactly $X^{-1/(a(G)-1)/a(G)}$ relative to the dominant $X^1$ count of $S_n$-fields). The two together exhibit the Abel-Ruffini threshold not as a binary fact (solvable vs. not) but as a measured *gradient* in field-counting space — the canonical contemporary lens on $S_5$ as the dominant Galois group of degree-5 number fields.
